Study of 281 Free Android VPN Apps Finds Traffic Leaks, Unencrypted Data, and Tracking

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 10 use cases 3 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Researchers ran 281 of the most popular free VPN apps on the Google Play Store through a new testing system and found that many fail at the basics people install a VPN for, i.e., keeping their traffic private and secure. The apps flagged with at least one problem have been installed more than 2.4 billion times. The problems are basic, not sophisticated. 29 apps let user traffic leak outside

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Endpoint carrying VPN library vulnerable to SWEET32 weak-cipher CVEs (Blowfish / 3DES)
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Android VPN app fetches OpenVPN config over cleartext HTTP (tunnel-hijack exposure)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DNS leak: Android endpoint queries public resolvers while VPN tunnel expected · [LLM] Android VPN/privacy app beaconing to advertising & analytics networks · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Android VPN app fetches OpenVPN config over cleartext HTTP (tunnel-hijack exposure) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts managed Android endpoints where a VPN/OpenVPN client downloads its .ovpn/.conf server-configuration file over plaintext HTTP (port 80) instead of HTTPS. This is the article's most serious finding: an on-path attacker (public Wi-Fi operator) can rewrite the cleartext config in transit and repoint the tunnel at an attacker-controlled server. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact tunnel-hijack mechanism: five apps download the config file in the clear so an attacker can redirect the connection. The .ovpn/.conf-over-port-80 pair is the concrete detectable artifact.
ATT&CKT1557 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate but poorly-engineered VPN apps that genuinely fetch config over HTTP (the true positive the study flags)
  • Non-VPN apps downloading files with .conf extension over HTTP (app updaters, config sync)
  • Corporate MDM pushing OpenVPN profiles over an internal HTTP mirror
  • Captive-portal redirects returning HTTP content before the tunnel is up
  • Security testing / MVPNalyzer-style research tooling on lab devices
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("com.microsoft.intune","com.company.mdm")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the Android package (InitiatingProcessFileName) and the RemoteUrl/host serving the config; confirm the response body is an OpenVPN profile and whether an HTTPS alternative exists. 2) Contain: if the app is on the flagged-apps list or serves config over HTTP on untrusted networks, block the app package via MDM/Intune and restrict the destination host at the egress firewall. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/IP across all Android devices, and search for the device subsequently routing traffic to an unexpected VPN endpoint IP (possible attacker-controlled server post-hijack).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemotePort == 80
| where RemoteUrl endswith ".ovpn" or RemoteUrl endswith ".conf" or (RemoteUrl has "openvpn" and RemoteUrl has "config")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where OSPlatform =~ "Android" | distinct DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ApplicationProtocol =~ "http" or DestinationPort == 80
| where RequestURL endswith ".ovpn" or RequestURL endswith ".conf" or (RequestURL has "openvpn" and RequestURL has "config")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, ApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS leak: Android endpoint queries public resolvers while VPN tunnel expected AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts DNS queries from managed Android devices sent directly to well-known public resolvers (Google, Cloudflare, Quad9, OpenDNS) on port 53, which indicates DNS traffic escaping the VPN tunnel. The study found 24 of 29 leaking apps expose DNS lookups to the local network, revealing which sites the user visits. Rationale: Uses the article's DNS-leak finding (traffic escaping the tunnel, exposing visited sites) anchored to concrete, well-known public-resolver IPs on port 53 — the observable signature of DNS that never entered the VPN tunnel.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1020
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Devices legitimately configured to use public DNS (private DNS / DNS-over-53 set to 8.8.8.8 by policy)
  • Apps with hardcoded resolver IPs that are unrelated to any VPN
  • Users not running a VPN at all — public resolver use is normal
  • Split-tunnel VPN configurations where DNS is intentionally sent outside the tunnel
  • Chromebook/Android hybrid devices using ISP-independent DNS by design
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("com.google.android.gms","com.android.chrome")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether a VPN app is active on the device at query time and whether org policy expects DNS to tunnel; identify the resolving package. 2) Contain: for high-risk users (censorship-region travelers), enforce a compliant VPN profile or block the leaking app via MDM. 3) Hunt: correlate the leaking device's cleartext DNS names with sensitive-site categories, and check whether the same app also appears in the cleartext-config or tracking-beacon detections.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 53
| where RemoteIP in ("8.8.8.8","8.8.4.4","1.1.1.1","1.0.0.1","9.9.9.9","149.112.112.112","208.67.222.222","208.67.220.220")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where OSPlatform =~ "Android" | distinct DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform) on DeviceId
| summarize QueryCount=count(), Resolvers=make_set(RemoteIP), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by QueryCount desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 53
| where DestinationIP in ("8.8.8.8","8.8.4.4","1.1.1.1","1.0.0.1","9.9.9.9","149.112.112.112","208.67.222.222","208.67.220.220")
| summarize QueryCount=count(), Resolvers=make_set(DestinationIP), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DeviceProduct
| order by QueryCount desc

Android VPN/privacy app beaconing to advertising & analytics networks AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts managed Android devices where apps (especially privacy/VPN apps) contact known advertising, analytics and attribution SDK endpoints. The study found 246 of 281 apps (>80%) contacted ad/tracking servers and 76 transmitted the device Advertising ID — directly contradicting the privacy pitch these apps make. Rationale: Anchored on the article's tracking finding (Advertising ID + >80% of apps contacting ad/analytics servers) using concrete, real-world SDK endpoint hostnames (AppsFlyer, Adjust, Mixpanel, Facebook Graph, Google Analytics) that these apps beacon to.
ATT&CKT1041 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate free apps whose monetization uses these same ad SDKs (extremely common on Android)
  • Google Analytics / Firebase telemetry from first-party corporate apps
  • Marketing-attribution beacons from sanctioned business apps
  • Games and social apps that legitimately embed AppsFlyer/Adjust
  • MDM-approved apps with disclosed analytics in their privacy policy
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating package; determine if it is a VPN/privacy app whose marketing claims no tracking, then check whether the Advertising ID or device identifiers are in the payload. 2) Contain: if a privacy/VPN app is exfiltrating identifiers against policy, flag it for removal via Intune/MDM app-protection policy. 3) Hunt: enumerate all Android apps contacting these SDK hosts, cross-reference against the study's flagged-app appendix, and prioritize any app that also appears in the DNS-leak or cleartext-config detections.
let TrackerHosts = dynamic(["graph.facebook.com","google-analytics.com","app-measurement.com","api.appsflyer.com","app.adjust.com","api.mixpanel.com","flurry.com","in.appcenter.ms"]);

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (TrackerHosts)
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where OSPlatform =~ "Android" | distinct DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform) on DeviceId
| summarize Trackers=make_set(RemoteUrl), Hits=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Hits desc
let TrackerHosts = dynamic(["graph.facebook.com","google-analytics.com","app-measurement.com","api.appsflyer.com","app.adjust.com","api.mixpanel.com","flurry.com"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName has_any (TrackerHosts) or RequestURL has_any (TrackerHosts)
| summarize Trackers=make_set(coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL)), Hits=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DeviceProduct
| order by Hits desc

Endpoint carrying VPN library vulnerable to SWEET32 weak-cipher CVEs (Blowfish / 3DES) AIWeaponization High
Surfaces managed devices whose installed software inventory carries the two weak-cipher CVEs the study calls out for the outdated Blowfish and Triple-DES ciphers bundled in poorly-maintained VPN OpenVPN configs. SWEET32 lets an attacker recover plaintext from long-running encrypted connections. Rationale: Uses the two exact CVE identifiers named in the article (CVE-2016-6329 for 64-bit-block Blowfish, CVE-2016-2183 SWEET32 for 3DES) against the TVM vulnerability inventory — a concrete, executable, low-FP match on the study's weak-tunnel-cipher finding.
ATT&CKT1600.001 T1040
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy internal VPN concentrators intentionally supporting 3DES for backward compatibility (accepted risk)
  • Third-party appliances where the CVE is flagged but the vulnerable cipher is disabled in config
  • TVM catalog attributing the CVE to a library present but not used for tunneling
  • Vendor software that has backported the fix without a version bump TVM recognizes
  • Test/lab devices deliberately running old OpenVPN builds
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the flagged SoftwareName/Version is actually a VPN/TLS library in active use and whether Blowfish/3DES is negotiated on live tunnels. 2) Contain: push the vendor's recommended security update or reconfigure the tunnel to a modern cipher (AES-GCM); block the weak cipher at the VPN gateway. 3) Hunt: enumerate all devices with the same SoftwareName across the fleet, and correlate with the cleartext-config and DNS-leak detections to identify wholesale use of a poorly-maintained free VPN app.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2016-6329","CVE-2016-2183")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), CVEs=make_set(CveId) by DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform
| order by LastSeen desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2016-6329","CVE-2016-2183")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), CVEs=make_set(CveId) by DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform
| order by LastSeen desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hackers Use Fake Microsoft Entra Passkey Enrollment to Gain Microsoft 365 Access

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 15 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A threat actor has been targeting organizations spanning multiple sectors with voice-based fake security requests that prompt Microsoft 365 users to enroll a new Entra passkey with an aim to carry out data extortion attacks. The threat actor, tracked by Okta under the moniker O-UNC-066, has deployed a panel-controlled phishing kit that's capable of targeting the passkey enrollment process. The

ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1555.003 T1566
Domainsassignpasskey.com deploypasskey.com passkeydeploy.com passkeyadd.com setpasskey.com

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Access to O-UNC-066 passkey-themed phishing kit domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Failed Entra sign-in burst followed by passkey-based success · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Entra ID passkey / FIDO2 security-key registration (O-UNC-066 rogue enrollment) · [LLM] Entra passkey enrollment from off-hours or never-before-seen IP · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Passkey registration immediately followed by passkey sign-in (rogue-enrollment account takeover) · [LLM] M365 sign-in with recently-enrolled passkey from new user-agent and IP · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Entra ID passkey / FIDO2 security-key registration (O-UNC-066 rogue enrollment) AIInstallation Medium
Surfaces every passkey/FIDO2 authentication-method registration in Entra ID so an analyst can validate it against a legitimate rollout. O-UNC-066 vishes users into approving the attacker's own passkey against their Microsoft 365 account, so a registration event is the pivotal artifact of this campaign. Rationale: Anchored on the article's core TTP — the attacker enrolls their own passkey after phone-guided MFA approval; a passkey/FIDO2 method-registration audit event is the durable artifact. Broad by design (hunting tier) because Microsoft's own passkey registration campaigns generate the same event. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/entra-passkey-enrollment-vishing-targets-microsoft-365-users/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/how-to-authentication-passkeys-fido2
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft/admin-driven passkey registration campaign nudging users to enroll (the article notes this feature coincides with the abuse)
  • Help-desk assisted passkey enrollment for a new hire
  • User self-enrolling a FIDO2 key from a corporate device during onboarding
  • Bulk FIDO2 provisioning via Graph/PowerShell (e.g. Token2 bulk enroll)
  • Passkey re-registration after device replacement
Suppression filter
| where ActorIP !in ("<corporate_egress_placeholder_do_not_use>") // prefer: exclude your admin bulk-enroll service principal by AccountObjectId once known
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the registering IP/UA and the target user; confirm the user actually initiated a passkey enrollment (call them out-of-band, do not use the same channel the attacker used). 2) Contain: if unrecognized, remove the newly-registered authentication method in Entra, revoke the user's refresh tokens/sessions, and force re-registration under a verified admin. 3) Hunt: check whether the same IP/UA registered passkeys for other users, and whether a passkey sign-in followed within minutes (see correlated UC).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application in~ ("Microsoft Entra ID","Office 365","Azure Active Directory")
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info","Register security information","Add passkey","security info")
| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","Passkey","security key")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, RawEventData
| sort by Timestamp desc
let RegOps = dynamic(["User registered security info","Admin registered security info","User started security info registration","User completed security info registration","Add passkey"]);
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName in~ (RegOps) or OperationName has "security info"
| where tostring(TargetResources) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","Passkey","security key")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Result, ResultReason, Actor, ActorIP, TargetResources
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: Entra ID Passkey or FIDO2 Authentication Method Registration
id: b3d1e5a2-7c94-4f2a-9c11-2a4f6e8b0d31
description: Detects registration of a passkey/FIDO2 security key as an Entra ID authentication method, the pivotal artifact of the O-UNC-066 rogue-passkey vishing campaign.
references:
  - https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hackers-use-fake-microsoft-entra.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.t1098.005
  - attack.t1556.006
logsource:
  product: azure
  service: auditlogs
detection:
  selection:
    OperationName|contains: 'security info'
  keywords:
    - 'Fido2'
    - 'passkey'
    - 'security key'
  condition: selection and keywords
level: medium
source:azure.activeDirectory (@evt.name:"User registered security info" OR @evt.name:"Add passkey" OR @action:*security\ info*) (*Fido2* OR *FIDO2* OR *passkey* OR *Passkey* OR *security\ key*)
Access to O-UNC-066 passkey-themed phishing kit domains AIDelivery High
Detects DNS/network connections to the named O-UNC-066 phishing infrastructure whose domains all embed the word 'passkey' (and per-target subdomains). This is the delivery stage where the victim is steered to the operator-controlled PHP kit that mimics the Entra passkey enrollment flow. Rationale: Uses the five named IOC domains confirmed by Okta and BleepingComputer; `has_any`/endswith on the registrable domain also catches the per-target subdomains (e.g. exampleentity.setpasskey.com). Named, corroborated infrastructure = high fidelity, low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/entra-passkey-enrollment-vishing-targets-microsoft-365-users/ • https://www.technadu.com/o-unc-066-vishing-campaign-abuses-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment/630640/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or SOC analyst intentionally browsing the IOC domain for analysis from a corporate host
  • Threat-intel sandbox/detonation VM resolving the domain
  • URL-scanning proxy or SWG pre-fetching the link
  • A benign passkey-vendor domain coincidentally matching the substring (verify exact registrable domain, not just substring)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and DeviceName !in~ ("soc-sandbox01","threat-detonation01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/host that resolved the domain and pull the surrounding sign-in and passkey-registration events for that user in the following hour. 2) Contain: block all five domains (and *.<domain>) at the SWG/DNS layer, revoke the user's tokens, and check for a newly-registered passkey to remove. 3) Hunt: sweep proxy/DNS org-wide for any of the five domains and for other passkey-substring domains registered recently; alert the user population targeted by the vishing calls.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("assignpasskey.com","deploypasskey.com","passkeydeploy.com","passkeyadd.com","setpasskey.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| sort by Timestamp desc
let PkDomains = dynamic(["assignpasskey.com","deploypasskey.com","passkeydeploy.com","passkeyadd.com","setpasskey.com"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (PkDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS Query to O-UNC-066 Passkey Phishing Domains
id: 6a2f0c74-1b8e-4d33-9a0e-7c5d2f1b9e40
description: Detects DNS resolution of the O-UNC-066 (Pink / CL-CRI-1147) passkey-enrollment phishing domains and their per-target subdomains.
references:
  - https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hackers-use-fake-microsoft-entra.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:

  - attack.t1583.001
logsource:

detection:
  selection:

      - 'assignpasskey.com'
      - 'deploypasskey.com'
      - 'passkeydeploy.com'
      - 'passkeyadd.com'
      - 'setpasskey.com'
  condition: selection

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 (@QueryName:(*assignpasskey.com OR *deploypasskey.com OR *passkeydeploy.com OR *passkeyadd.com OR *setpasskey.com) OR @DestinationHostname:(*assignpasskey.com OR *deploypasskey.com OR *passkeydeploy.com OR *passkeyadd.com OR *setpasskey.com))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(assignpasskey|deploypasskey|passkeydeploy|passkeyadd|setpasskey)\.com$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*assignpasskey.com" OR DNS.query="*deploypasskey.com" OR DNS.query="*passkeydeploy.com" OR DNS.query="*passkeyadd.com" OR DNS.query="*setpasskey.com") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*assignpasskey.com" OR DNS.query="*deploypasskey.com" OR DNS.query="*passkeydeploy.com" OR DNS.query="*passkeyadd.com" OR DNS.query="*setpasskey.com") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Passkey registration immediately followed by passkey sign-in (rogue-enrollment account takeover) AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates an Entra passkey/FIDO2 method registration with a successful passkey-based sign-in by the same principal within 15 minutes. O-UNC-066 registers its own passkey and then immediately authenticates with it to take over the M365 account, so tight temporal linkage is high-fidelity. Rationale: Encodes the article's exact sequence: register attacker passkey, then use it. The 15-minute join eliminates the vast majority of benign enrollments (which are rarely used to sign in seconds later) and pins the takeover. RegIP vs sign-in IP surfaces the operator/victim split described in the kit walkthrough. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hackers-use-fake-microsoft-entra.html
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User enrolls a passkey and legitimately tests it by signing in right away
  • Onboarding flow that enrolls then immediately authenticates the new key
  • Admin registers a key on behalf of a user during an assisted session and validates it
  • Conditional-access registration campaign that requires an immediate re-auth
Suppression filter
| where IPAddress != RegIP // keep only enroll-then-signin where the sign-in comes from a different IP than the registration
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare RegIP and sign-in IPAddress/geo — a mismatch or datacenter/VPN ASN strongly indicates the operator model described by Okta. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/refresh tokens, disable the account, and delete the just-registered passkey; require verified in-person/out-of-band re-enrollment. 3) Hunt: check the target app (Exchange/SharePoint/Teams) for post-auth mailbox rule creation, data access, or download bursts consistent with the data-extortion objective.
let Reg = CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info","Register security information","Add passkey","security info")
| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","security key")
| project RegTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, RegIP = IPAddress;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationDetails) has_any ("FIDO2","Passkey","Windows Hello")
| join kind=inner Reg on AccountObjectId
| where Timestamp between (RegTime .. RegTime + 15m)
| project RegTime, SignInTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, RegIP, IPAddress, Country, Application, DeltaMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, RegTime)
| sort by SignInTime desc
let Reg = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName has "security info" and tostring(TargetResources) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","security key")
| project RegTime = TimeGenerated, UserId = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.id), Upn = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), RegIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationMethodsUsed) has_any ("FIDO2","Passkey","Windows Hello")
| join kind=inner Reg on $left.UserId == $right.UserId
| where TimeGenerated between (RegTime .. RegTime + 15m)
| project RegTime, SignInTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, RegIP, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, DeltaMin = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, RegTime)
| sort by SignInTime desc
Entra passkey enrollment from off-hours or never-before-seen IP AIInstallation Medium
Flags passkey/FIDO2 registration events where the enrolling IP has not been seen for that user in the 30-day sign-in baseline, or the enrollment happens outside business hours. Targets the anomaly in the enrollment event itself rather than a follow-on sign-in. Rationale: Reviewer-requested anomaly view. The article's vishing calls occur opportunistically and the operator's IP will not match the victim's normal sign-in geography; a new-IP or off-hours passkey enrollment is a concrete deviation from legitimate self-service enrollment. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Traveling/remote employee enrolling a passkey from a hotel/home IP not in baseline
  • Shift worker or on-call staff enrolling legitimately at night
  • New hire whose IP baseline is thin/empty
  • Enrollment via corporate VPN egress that differs from prior sign-in IPs
  • Org-wide passkey campaign rolled out after hours to reduce user disruption
Suppression filter
| where NewIP == true // prioritize new-IP enrollments; drop the pure off-hours clause first if the org runs after-hours campaigns
Response runbook
1) Triage: geolocate RegIP and check the ASN — residential/VPN/datacenter far from the user's norm plus a recent vishing report escalates severity. 2) Contain: if unverified, delete the passkey, revoke tokens, and confirm with the user via a trusted channel. 3) Hunt: query AuditLogs for other passkey enrollments from the same RegIP/ASN across the tenant to find additional victims in the same campaign.
let Known = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize by AccountObjectId, IPAddress;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info","Register security information","Add passkey","security info")
| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","security key")
| extend HourUTC = hourofday(Timestamp)
| join kind=leftouter Known on AccountObjectId, IPAddress
| extend NewIP = isempty(IPAddress1)
| where NewIP or HourUTC >= 22 or HourUTC < 6
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, NewIP, HourUTC, ActionType
| sort by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 30d;
let KnownIPs = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(1d))
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize by UserId, IPAddress;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where OperationName has "security info" and tostring(TargetResources) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","security key")
| extend UserId = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.id), Upn = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), RegIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| extend HourUTC = hourofday(TimeGenerated), Day = dayofweek(TimeGenerated)
| join kind=leftouter (KnownIPs) on $left.UserId == $right.UserId, $left.RegIP == $right.IPAddress
| extend NewIP = isempty(IPAddress)
| where NewIP or HourUTC >= 22 or HourUTC < 6 or Day == 0d or Day == 6d  // off-hours (UTC) or weekend; adjust to org timezone
| project TimeGenerated, Upn, RegIP, NewIP, HourUTC, Day, OperationName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
Failed Entra sign-in burst followed by passkey-based success AIExploitation Medium
Detects an account with 3+ failed sign-ins in a 2-hour window that then produces a successful passkey/FIDO2 sign-in within 24 hours. Models the O-UNC-066 pattern of harvesting/validating credentials via the kit before the attacker-registered passkey grants durable access. Rationale: Ties the article's credential-harvesting kit (username/password captured to /backend.php) to the durable passkey outcome. A failed-auth cluster preceding a passkey success is a strong takeover shape that a plain passkey sign-in alone would miss. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://www.scworld.com/news/okta-warns-of-vishing-scheme-that-extorts-data
ATT&CKT1110 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User fat-fingers password several times then signs in with their legitimate passkey
  • Stale cached credentials on a second device causing failures before passkey use
  • Password-expiry period generating failures ahead of passwordless enrollment
  • MFA prompt timeouts logged as failures before a successful passkey auth
Suppression filter
| where SuccessIP !in (FailIPs) // keep cases where the passkey success comes from a different IP than the failed attempts
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare FailIPs to SuccessIP — different geo/ASN between the failures and the passkey success is the key escalator. 2) Contain: revoke tokens, disable the account, and audit the account's registered passkeys, removing any not verified with the user. 3) Hunt: pivot on FailIPs across the tenant for password-spray/enumeration against other users, and check for passkey registrations from those IPs.
let Failed = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode != 0
| summarize FailCount = count(), FailIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstFail = min(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 2h)
| where FailCount >= 3;  // 3+ failed auths in a 2h bucket = probing
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationDetails) has_any ("FIDO2","Passkey")
| join kind=inner Failed on AccountObjectId
| where Timestamp between (FirstFail .. FirstFail + 24h)
| project FirstFail, SuccessTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, FailCount, FailIPs, SuccessIP = IPAddress, Country, Application
| sort by SuccessTime desc
let Failed = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType !in (0)
| summarize FailCount = count(), FailIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, UserId, bin(TimeGenerated, 2h)
| where FailCount >= 3;  // 3+ failed auths in a 2h window
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationMethodsUsed) has_any ("FIDO2","Passkey")
| join kind=inner Failed on UserId
| where TimeGenerated between (FirstFail .. FirstFail + 24h)
| project FirstFail, SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, FailCount, FailIPs, SuccessIP = IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName
| sort by SuccessTime desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:0 (*FIDO2* OR *Passkey*)
M365 sign-in with recently-enrolled passkey from new user-agent and IP AIActions on Objectives Medium
Alerts when a successful passkey/FIDO2 sign-in uses a passkey enrolled in the last 24 hours and originates from a user-agent + IP combination never seen for that user in the 30-day baseline. Captures the attacker operating the fraudulently-enrolled passkey from their own browser/device. Rationale: Reviewer-requested. Combines three weak signals into a sharp one: passkey <24h old (fresh rogue enrollment), plus a UA+IP tuple absent from the user's baseline (attacker's own environment). Leftanti baseline expresses 'first-time observed' without ML. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/entra-passkey-enrollment-vishing-targets-microsoft-365-users/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User enrolls a passkey then signs in from a new personal laptop/browser (new UA+IP) legitimately
  • User travels and first uses the new passkey from a hotel/airport IP
  • Browser or OS update changing the user-agent string right after enrollment
  • BYOD device newly used with a corporate passkey
  • Thin baseline for a recently onboarded user
Suppression filter
| where Country != "<home_country_iso_placeholder>" // optional geo refinement; safer to keep UA+IP baseline leftanti as the primary filter
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect UserAgent and IP geo/ASN; a datacenter/VPN ASN or foreign geo on a fresh passkey is high-signal. 2) Contain: revoke tokens, remove the recently-registered passkey, and require verified re-enrollment; enforce a conditional-access session control on the user. 3) Hunt: review the target application activity (mailbox rules, SharePoint/OneDrive downloads, Teams data access) for the data-extortion follow-on this actor is known for.
let RecentReg = CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(2d)
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info","Register security information","Add passkey","security info")
| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","security key")
| summarize RegTime = max(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId;
let Baseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize by AccountObjectId, UserAgent, IPAddress;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationDetails) has_any ("FIDO2","Passkey")
| join kind=inner RecentReg on AccountObjectId
| where Timestamp between (RegTime .. RegTime + 24h)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountObjectId, UserAgent, IPAddress
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, UserAgent, Country, Application, RegTime
| sort by Timestamp desc
let RecentReg = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2d)
| where OperationName has "security info" and tostring(TargetResources) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","security key")
| summarize RegTime = max(TimeGenerated) by UserId = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.id);
let Baseline = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize by UserId, UserAgent, IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationMethodsUsed) has_any ("FIDO2","Passkey")
| join kind=inner RecentReg on UserId
| where TimeGenerated between (RegTime .. RegTime + 24h)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on UserId, UserAgent, IPAddress
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, UserAgent, Location, AppDisplayName, RegTime
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")

          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'

falsepositives:

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents

ImFileEvent

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

logsource:

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

Attackers Exploit 'Ill Bloom' Vulnerability to Drain Over $5 Million From Cryptocurrency Wallets

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 6 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Security firm&nbsp;Coinspect&nbsp;has disclosed a crypto wallet flaw it calls&nbsp;Ill Bloom, and attackers are already using it. The flaw is in how some wallet software generated its recovery phrase, the words that control the money. When that phrase is made with weak randomness, an attacker can work it out and take everything it controls. The firm has confirmed one coordinated sweep on May 27

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1486 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.

ImRegistryEvent

| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/

    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access

    category: file_access
    product: windows

            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:

            - '\Cookies'

status: experimental
description: |

    activity.

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

YesWiki Bazar CalcField formula RCE: PHP command-exec functions in HTTP request (CVE-2026-52778) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to a YesWiki Bazar form/CalcField handler whose formula payload contains PHP command-execution primitives (system(), passthru(), shell_exec(), exec(), base64_decode()) — the Scenario-B RCE payload `abs(1) + system('id')` that slips past the flawed recursive-regex sanitizer into eval(). Article-specific because it keys on the Bazar path plus the exact PHP sinks the write-up names, not generic web attacks. Rationale: Anchors on the exact Bazar/CalcField sink and the PHP command-exec functions named in the article's Scenario-B PoC (`system('id')`); combining the 'bazar' path token with a PHP execution primitive is extremely rare in legitimate math-formula traffic, giving high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52778 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52778/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-52778
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Bazar wiki page whose text content or form label literally contains the word 'exec' or 'system' in prose being saved via GET-encoded form data
  • Security scanners / pentest tools (Nikto, Nuclei CVE-2026-52778 template) probing the endpoint from an authorized source IP
  • Developer testing the CalcField patch with benign formula strings that happen to include function-like tokens
  • WAF that logs the full decoded body producing the same signature twice (allow + block events)
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "Nuclei" and RequestClientApplication !has "Nikto" and SourceIP !in ("<authorized-scanner-ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request (URL + body) and the DestinationHostName; confirm the target is a YesWiki host < 4.6.6 and check the web/PHP error log at the same timestamp for eval() output. Identify SourceIP and whether the request returned 200. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, take the YesWiki instance offline or virtual-patch the Bazar endpoint, and rotate any secrets in .env readable by www-data. 3) Hunt: pivot to endpoint process telemetry for php-fpm/apache spawning shells (UC3) on that host, review outbound connections from the web account, and grep the webroot for newly written PHP files (webshells).
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "bazar" or RequestContext has "bazar"
| extend Payload = strcat(tostring(RequestURL), " ", tostring(RequestContext), " ", tostring(Message))
| where Payload has_any ("system(","passthru(","shell_exec(","exec(","base64_decode(","proc_open(")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DeviceProduct, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki CalcField ReDoS: deeply nested-parenthesis formula payload (CVE-2026-52778) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to a YesWiki Bazar/CalcField handler carrying a formula with a long run of nested/open parentheses — the Scenario-A ReDoS/PCRE stack-overflow payload `((((...1+1...))))` (multiplied 2000–5000x) that crashes the PHP-FPM worker. Article-specific: the recursive `(?1)+` regex plus thousands of open parens is the exact DoS vector described. Rationale: The article's Scenario-A payload is a literal run of thousands of `(` sent to the Bazar CalcField; a 20+ open-paren run (raw or URL-encoded %28) on that path is a non-ambiguous signature of the ReDoS/stack-overflow attempt and essentially never occurs in benign math formulas. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52778 • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-52778
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated vulnerability scanners firing the public CVE-2026-52778 ReDoS test payload from an authorized source
  • A genuinely complex but legitimate nested math formula authored by a power user (rare beyond ~5 nesting levels)
  • Fuzzing / QA tooling run by the app team against a staging YesWiki host
  • WAF logging the same oversized request on both the allow and block pass
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<authorized-scanner-ip>") and DeviceAction != "allowed-staging"
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the request timestamp with PHP-FPM/Apache worker crashes or 5xx spikes and host CPU on the YesWiki server; count open parens to confirm intent vs. a legit formula. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP, enable a WAF rule limiting request body length / paren count to the Bazar endpoint, and confirm PHP `pcre.recursion_limit`/stack limits; upgrade to YesWiki 4.6.6. 3) Hunt: check for repeated bursts from the same IP/subnet (sustained DoS), and verify the same actor did not also send the Scenario-B RCE payload (UC1).

| where RequestURL has "bazar" or RequestContext has "bazar"
| extend Payload = strcat(tostring(RequestURL), " ", tostring(RequestContext), " ", tostring(Message))
| where Payload matches regex @"(\(|%28){20,}"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DeviceProduct, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki RCE landing: web-server (php-fpm/apache) spawning shell or recon commands (CVE-2026-52778) AIExploitation High
Hunts a YesWiki web-server process (php-fpm, apache2, httpd, nginx) spawning a shell or reconnaissance binary (sh, bash, id, whoami, uname, cat, curl, wget) as the www-data/apache account — the post-eval() code-execution landing where `system('id')` runs under the web user. Article-specific because it targets the exact www-data privilege context and command (`id`) the write-up shows. Rationale: Directly targets the article's Scenario-B outcome — `system('id')` executed under the www-data web user — by pairing a YesWiki web-server parent with a shell/recon child; the parent→child pair plus the web service account is a high-fidelity RCE-confirmation signal. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52778 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52778/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Server monitoring/health-check plugins that run `uname`/`id` from PHP
  • Cron or deploy scripts running as www-data invoking bash wrappers
  • Composer/package tooling executed under the web account during maintenance
Suppression filter

| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git ","composer","convert ","/healthcheck") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child and the parent php-fpm command; confirm the host is YesWiki < 4.6.6 and correlate with a UC1/UC2 web hit in the preceding seconds. Determine if the command is recon (id/whoami) or download (curl/wget of a second stage). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending php-fpm worker, block outbound from the web account, and rotate www-data-readable secrets. 3) Hunt: search FileWritten/DeviceFileEvents for new .php files under the webroot (webshells), review crontab and SUID changes for persistence, and sweep other internet-facing YesWiki hosts for the same parent→child pattern.

YesWiki CVE-2026-52777 BazarImport POST to ?BazaR&vue=importer (CSRF exploit request) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound HTTP POST requests to the YesWiki BazaR importer endpoint (`?BazaR&vue=importer&id_typeannonce=<N>`) carrying the `importfiche` parameter — the exact request shape that reaches the CSRF-able `CSVManager::importEntry` unserialize sink. Article-specific because it keys on the literal action route and POST parameter, not a generic web-import template; a cross-site Referer or missing CSRF token on this route is the CVE-2026-52777 tell. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploit route `?BazaR&vue=importer&id_typeannonce=` and the `importfiche` POST parameter from BazarImportAction::formatArguments(); the CSRF path means the request will often carry an external Referer, which raises fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9369-69wj-7m2f • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/
ATT&CKT1190 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate wiki admin performing a genuine Bazar CSV import via the UI
  • Automated content-migration scripts that batch-import Bazar entries
  • Security scanners / vuln management probing the importer endpoint
  • Same-origin admin activity where Referer is the wiki itself (filter with CrossSiteRef)
Suppression filter
| where CrossSiteRef == "cross-site" or isempty(Referer)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request — decode the `importfiche[0]` value; if it base64-decodes to a PHP-serialized blob (`a:`/`O:` prefix) it is an exploit attempt, benign UI imports send CSV rows not serialized objects. Check Referer/source IP against known admin workstations. 2) Contain: if the request succeeded (2xx) treat the host as potentially RCE-compromised — isolate the web server, invalidate all admin sessions, and rotate the admin credential. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to php-fpm/apache child-process spawns and new `.php` file writes in the web root within minutes of this request; confirm YesWiki is >= 4.6.6.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "BazaR" and Url has "vue=importer"
| extend Referer = column_ifexists("HttpRequestHeaderReferer", "")
| extend CrossSiteRef = iff(Referer matches regex @"(?i)^https?://" and not(Referer has DstHostname), "cross-site", "same-site-or-none")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent = column_ifexists("HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent",""), Referer, CrossSiteRef
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki BazarImport base64 PHP-serialized object payload in POST body (PHPGGC gadget) AIExploitation High
Higher-fidelity variant that inspects the request body for the `importfiche` parameter carrying a base64 blob that decodes to a PHP-serialized object — i.e. a PHPGGC Doctrine/RCE1 or FW1 gadget chain. Keys on the serialized-object base64 signatures (`Tzo` = `O:`, `YTox`/`YToy` = `a:1:`/`a:2:`) seen in the advisory PoC payload, so it fires on the actual deserialization exploit rather than benign CSV imports. Rationale: Combines the article's `importfiche` parameter with the base64 signatures of PHP-serialized objects (`Tzo`=`O:`, `YToxOnt`=`a:1:{`) matching the verbatim PoC payload `YToxOntpOjA7Tzo2...`; benign CSV imports never carry serialized objects, giving low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9369-69wj-7m2f • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc
ATT&CKT1190 T1027
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A pentester/red-team validating CVE-2026-52777 with a real PHPGGC payload (true positive that is authorised)
  • Security researcher sending the advisory's exact PoC base64 marker for testing
  • WAF logging a blocked deserialization attempt (still worth alerting — attack occurred)
  • Rare CSV cell content that coincidentally base64-matches the serialized signature (mitigated by requiring the importfiche param)
Response runbook
1) Triage: base64-decode the captured `importfiche` value; confirm it deserializes to a PHP object graph (look for `O:<len>:"<class>"` and Doctrine gadget class names). 2) Contain: assume RCE if the server responded 2xx — isolate the web host, kill/rotate the web-app service account, invalidate admin sessions, and snapshot for forensics before rebuild. 3) Hunt: correlate with php-fpm/apache spawning a shell and web-shell `.php` writes within 2s of this request; sweep other admin accounts and shared-hosting neighbours mentioned as pivot targets in the advisory.

| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "vue=importer" or Message has "vue=importer"
