YesWiki object-injection RCE: php-fpm/apache spawns shell (Doctrine/RCE1 system()) AIExploitation High
Detects a PHP web-server process (php-fpm, php, php-cgi, httpd, apache2, or w3wp hosting PHP) spawning a command shell — the terminal behaviour of the PHPGGC Doctrine/RCE1 gadget that ends in `system($cmd)` after CVE-2026-52777 deserialization. Article-specific because the advisory names the RCE1 gadget and the sink executes in the web-server process context. Rationale: The advisory states the Doctrine/RCE1 gadget terminates in `system($cmd)`; a web-server PHP process spawning sh/bash/cmd is the highest-fidelity post-exploitation signal and named binaries make this alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9369-69wj-7m2f • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • YesWiki/PHP app legitimately shelling out (e.g. ImageMagick, git, or backup cron invoked via exec)
  • Composer/plugin install running shell commands as the web user
  • Server monitoring plugins that call system utilities
  • Admin debugging via a PHP web shell they deployed intentionally
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","gs","gm","/usr/bin/git","composer"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child process command line — benign PHP shell-outs are narrow known utilities; arbitrary `sh -c`, recon (`id`,`whoami`,`uname`), or download commands (`curl`,`wget`) indicate exploitation. Correlate timestamp with a preceding `vue=importer` POST. 2) Contain: isolate the web host, terminate the shell tree, suspend the web-app service account, and preserve memory/disk. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by the web user (web shells, cron entries), check outbound connections from the PHP process, and confirm all YesWiki instances are patched to 4.6.6.

ImProcessCreate

| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","php-cgi.exe","httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe") or ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","php-cgi.exe","httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe")

YesWiki BazarImport RCE: PHP process writes web shell or tampers wakka.config.php AIInstallation Medium
Detects the YesWiki web-server process writing a `.php` file into the web root or modifying `wakka.config.php` — the outcome of the PHPGGC Doctrine/FW1 gadget (`file_put_contents($php_file, $contents)`) and the persistence actions the advisory explicitly calls out (web shells, wakka.config.php modification). Article-specific through the named config file and the FW1 file-write primitive. Rationale: Uses the advisory's named `wakka.config.php` config file and the Doctrine/FW1 `file_put_contents($php_file)` primitive; a web-server PHP process writing a new .php outside cache/tmp is a strong web-shell indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9369-69wj-7m2f • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • YesWiki extension/theme installation writing new .php files under the web root
  • Legitimate admin editing wakka.config.php via the wiki configuration UI
  • YesWiki cache/compiled-template regeneration (mitigated by excluding cache/tmp paths)
  • Composer autoloader regeneration during an upgrade
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "/tools/" and FolderPath !has "/vendor/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written file — a small file with `eval`, `system`, `assert`, `base64_decode`, or `$_POST`/`$_GET` handlers is a web shell; diff wakka.config.php against the last known-good backup for injected handlers or altered secrets. 2) Contain: remove/quarantine the file, block web access to it, rotate any secrets exposed in wakka.config.php (DB creds), and invalidate admin sessions. 3) Hunt: search web access logs for GETs to the new .php filename (attacker interaction), review all files owned by the web user modified in the exploit window, and confirm the YesWiki upgrade to 4.6.6.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","php","php-cgi.exe","httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName =~ "wakka.config.php"

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","php-cgi.exe","httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php" or TargetFileName =~ "wakka.config.php"
| where TargetFilePath !has "/cache/" and TargetFilePath !has "/tmp/"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki deserialization exploit failures in PHP/web error logs (unserialize / __destruct) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts PHP or web-server error logs for the deserialization exploit's failure fingerprints — `unserialize` warnings, magic-method errors, and specifically the PoC's `Object of class ... could not be converted to string` message thrown by the `array_map('strval', $entry)` line at CSVManager.php:373. Failed or version-mismatched PHPGGC chains against CVE-2026-52777 surface here, often repeating as the attacker retries. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim PoC error `Object of class Gadget could not be converted to string` produced by the CSVManager `array_map('strval', $entry)` line, plus `unserialize`/`__destruct` magic-method fingerprints — exactly what a failed or mistuned gadget chain emits. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9369-69wj-7m2f
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated PHP plugin bugs that legitimately call unserialize and warn on malformed data
  • Developers running/debugging code that emits __destruct or serialization notices
  • Batch import of a genuinely malformed (but non-malicious) CSV/serialized cache file
  • Noisy verbose logging levels producing routine deprecation notices
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("could not be converted to string", "unserialize")
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the error timestamp with web access logs for a `vue=importer` POST from the same source IP; a burst of these errors near an importer request indicates active exploitation attempts. 2) Contain: if paired with a successful (2xx) import request, treat as compromise — isolate host and rotate the web-app service account. 3) Hunt: enumerate retry attempts (repeated errors) to gauge attacker persistence, then pivot to php->shell spawns and new .php writes on the same host; verify YesWiki is patched to 4.6.6 which removes the serialized-transport path.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","apache2","httpd")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("unserialize", "could not be converted to string", "__destruct", "__wakeup", "Object of class")
| summarize Count = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Sample = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, ProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc

YesWiki bulk page deletion via {{erasespamedcomments}} — audit-log deletion burst AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a burst of YesWiki 'Suppression de la page' administrative-action log entries in a short window, the ground-truth impact signal of CVE-2026-52766 where a single POST with a multi-element suppr[] array deletes many wiki pages at once. Keys on the exact French audit string LogAdministrativeAction writes for each deleted tag. Rationale: Uses the exact 'Suppression de la page' string that PageController::delete() -> LogAdministrativeAction writes for every deleted tag; a burst of >=3 in 5 minutes reflects the suppr[] array bulk-delete described in the article and CVSS A:H impact. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52766/
ATT&CKT1485
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin decommissioning a section of the wiki and deleting several pages in one sitting
  • Site migration or content restructuring where old pages are pruned in bulk
  • Genuine spam cleanup by an authorized moderator using the same action against real spam pages
  • Automated maintenance/cron job that prunes stale draft pages
Suppression filter
| where DeletedPages >= 3
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SamplePages set and confirm whether high-value tags (PagePrincipale, admin/config pages) were deleted; check the web/WAF log for the source IP of the POST to the trigger page immediately preceding the burst. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the wiki read-only, and restore deleted rows from the latest DB backup (pages/links/acls/triples/referrers/tags). 3) Hunt: confirm YesWiki version <4.6.6, search for anonymously-created trigger pages containing '{{erasespamedcomments}}', and review for other unauth actions from the same IP.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where SyslogMessage has "Suppression de la page"     // exact LogAdministrativeAction string per deleted tag
| summarize DeletedPages = dcount(SyslogMessage), SamplePages = make_set(SyslogMessage, 15), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, HostName, HostIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DeletedPages >= 3     // 3+ page deletions in 5 min = suppr[] array abuse, not routine one-off admin cleanup
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.syslog "Suppression de la page"

YesWiki CVE-2026-52766 exploit request — erasespamedcomments clean=yes suppr[] POST AIExploitation Medium
Detects the exploitation POST for CVE-2026-52766 in WAF/web request logs: a POST carrying the erasespamedcomments action together with the clean=yes flag and a suppr[] array. Requires request-body inspection on the WAF (the parameters live in the POST body, not the URL query string). Rationale: Keys on the three attacker-controlled strings from the article PoC (erasespamedcomments action name, clean=yes flag, suppr[] array); the combination is not produced by normal wiki browsing/editing. Confidence is Medium because the params sit in the POST body, so it only fires where the WAF logs request bodies. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52766/
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An authorized moderator legitimately running the erasespamedcomments spam-cleanup action against genuine spam pages
  • WAF/vulnerability scanners (Nuclei, Burp) probing for CVE-2026-52766 in an authorized pentest
  • Security team validating the 4.6.6 patch with a benign reproduction request
  • Log-replay or SIEM test harness re-ingesting the PoC payload
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the suppr[] tags in the body to see which pages were targeted (PagePrincipale = front page) and check the response code/size to gauge success; verify the source IP is not an authorized admin. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF and add a WAF rule denying POSTs containing clean=yes+suppr[] to unauthenticated sessions; upgrade YesWiki to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: correlate with Syslog 'Suppression de la page' entries within 60s to confirm pages were actually deleted, and review the same IP for other YesWiki CVEs from this advisory batch (SQLi, SSRF, eval RCE).

UAT-7810 ORB network C2 beacon to known relay IPs (LONGLEASH/DOGLEASH) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host or edge device communicating with the four UAT-7810 command-and-control / Operational Relay Box IPs used by the LONGLEASH intermediate C2 relay and DOGLEASH backdoors. These IPs also carried the ASUS AiCloud exploitation (217.15.164.147), so a hit is either inbound exploitation or outbound C2 for this specific China-nexus ORB campaign. Rationale: Anchored on the four UAT-7810 C2/ORB IPs (194.233.92.26, 217.15.160.247, 217.15.164.147, 95.182.100.231) and ports 99/2222/8088 confirmed across the Talos report and BleepingComputer/THN — pure-IOC match on second-source-confirmed infrastructure, so any hit is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/china-linked-uat-7810-expands-orb.html
ATT&CKT1090.001 T1071.001 T1571

  • Internal threat-intel/red-team validation deliberately connecting to the IOC IPs
  • A shared-hosting IP later re-purposed to a benign service after Talos publication
  • Security scanner/EDR sandbox detonating a sample and reaching out to the C2
  • Passive DNS or netflow research tooling touching the range
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal asset and process (InitiatingProcessFileName) that talked to the IOC IP; confirm direction — inbound to an internet-facing Ruckus/ASUS edge device is likely exploitation, outbound from a host is likely C2. 2) Contain: block all four IPs at perimeter/EDR, isolate the endpoint or quarantine the edge device, and capture volatile memory/config from the router before power-cycling. 3) Hunt: pivot on the asset for leash-family file hashes (see companion UC), sweep firewall logs for the other three C2 IPs and ports 99/2222/8088 org-wide, and check whether the device was proxying traffic between unrelated external IP pairs (ORB relay behavior).

Ruckus/ASUS edge routers exposed to UAT-7810 n-day exploit CVEs AIExploitation High
Surfaces internet-facing Ruckus and ASUS AiCloud devices carrying the exact n-day CVEs UAT-7810 exploits for initial access into its ORB network. This is exposure hunting for the specific vulnerability set (CVE-2020-22653, CVE-2020-22658, CVE-2023-25717, CVE-2025-2492) named in the campaign, not a generic patch report. Rationale: Uses the four exact CVE IDs Talos ties to UAT-7810 initial access (Ruckus CVE-2020-22653/22658/2023-25717, ASUS AiCloud CVE-2025-2492), confirmed by THN/SecurityWeek — turns a generic patch gap into campaign-specific attack-surface hunting. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/ • https://www.securityweek.com/china-linked-apt-expands-arsenal-with-new-leash-backdoors/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/china-linked-uat-7810-expands-orb.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scanner flags an already-patched device due to stale banner/version fingerprint
  • Device is Ruckus/ASUS-branded but the vulnerable web-admin service is not network-reachable
  • Lab/decommissioned router kept intentionally unpatched
  • CVE present but device is behind segmentation and not internet-facing (lower priority, not a true FP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device is genuinely running the vulnerable Ruckus Wireless Admin (<=10.4) or ASUS AiCloud firmware and whether its management interface is internet-reachable. 2) Contain: patch/firmware-upgrade or ACL the management interface off the internet immediately; for CVE-2023-25717 (unauth RCE via a single HTTP GET) treat any exposed device as presumed-compromised. 3) Hunt: cross-check the device's public IP against inbound connections from the four UAT-7810 C2 IPs, inspect the router for leash-family binaries and unexpected listeners on ports 99/2222/8088, and review whether it has been relaying traffic between unrelated external hosts.

LONGLEASH / JARLEASH / LEASHTEST malware hash sighting on managed hosts AIInstallation Medium
Alerts when a file matching a confirmed UAT-7810 leash-family SHA256 (LONGLEASH relay, JARLEASH admin tool, LEASHTEST utility) is written or executed on a managed host or Linux/edge sensor. Catches staging, cross-compilation, or a jump-host used to deploy the router implants for this ORB campaign. Rationale: Uses three second-source-confirmed leash-family SHA256s from the Talos IOC bundle (LONGLEASH 755fcee…, LEASHTEST 1b5649…, JARLEASH 324d95…); exact-hash matches are near-zero-FP and specific to this campaign's toolset. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/
ATT&CKT1105 T1090.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware sample sitting on a reverse-engineer/IR analyst workstation
  • AV/EDR quarantine copy of the file being re-hashed
  • Threat-intel platform caching the sample for detonation
  • Backup/archive process copying a captured forensic image
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("malware","sandbox","forensic","ir-lab") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is not a sanctioned malware-analysis box; capture file path, the writing process, and the account. Note these are MIPS/ARM/Linux router binaries, so a Windows hit almost always means a staging/build host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the binary, and hash-block it across EDR. 3) Hunt: from that host, pivot to outbound connections to the four UAT-7810 C2 IPs, look for JARLEASH's FTP/SFTP/Netcat listeners and DOGLEASH's hardcoded-port listeners, and review whether any edge routers were reached from this host over SSH/HTTP for implant deployment.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)

    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort

| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised @injectivelabs/sdk-ts exfiltrates wallet keys through fake telemetry

Aikido
2026-07-09 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A malicious release of @injectivelabs/sdk-ts hid a wallet-key stealer inside code labeled as usage telemetry, then spread it across 17 more npm packages. Here's how it worked and how to check your projects. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Transitive install of poisoned @injectivelabs 1.20.21 build under node_modules
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Compromised @injectivelabs/sdk-ts exfiltrates wallet keys through fake telemetry
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious @injectivelabs SDK build artifact by SHA-256 on disk · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Exfil to lookalike Injective gRPC-web subdomain (@injectivelabs stealer C2) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Exfil to lookalike Injective gRPC-web subdomain (@injectivelabs stealer C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound DNS/network activity to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network, the character-code-rebuilt exfil host used by the trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 to smuggle base64 wallet key material inside an X-Request-Id header disguised as gRPC-web traffic. Article-specific because the FQDN is a fixed IOC unique to this campaign. Rationale: The exfil FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network is a fixed, campaign-unique IOC (a lookalike subdomain never served by real Injective infra); matching it exactly avoids the FP risk of the parent injective.network.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1132.001 T1041 T1001.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate future Injective testnet archival endpoint being stood up under this exact FQDN (verify DNS/PKI ownership)
  • Security tooling / sandbox detonating the malicious package intentionally
  • Threat-intel sinkhole or research VM deliberately resolving the IOC
  • Internal DNS logging replaying old cached queries
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving host ran an @injectivelabs-dependent app; capture the initiating process (node.exe) and user. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat every wallet mnemonic/private key derived on it as exposed — freeze/rotate. 3) Hunt: pivot to all hosts querying the FQDN, pull package-lock/yarn.lock for @injectivelabs/*@1.20.21, and search DeviceFileEvents for the two malicious build artifacts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious @injectivelabs SDK build artifact by SHA-256 on disk AIInstallation Medium
Detects the two poisoned build files (accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) from @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 landing on disk, matched on their exact SHA-256 hashes. High fidelity IOC match that survives file renaming. Rationale: Both SHA-256 values are published IOCs for the exact malicious build artifacts; a hash match is unambiguous and near-zero FP, catching the stealer even if the file is renamed during transitive install.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / malware analyst intentionally storing the sample
  • Backup or EDR quarantine copy of the artifact triggering a second file event
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion writing the IOC file to a sandbox share
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and host; confirm whether it is a dev/CI machine or an analyst sandbox. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the affected node_modules, and pin @injectivelabs/* to a clean version (>=1.20.23); treat any wallet keys handled on the host as compromised. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints/CI runners for the same hashes and for outbound contact to the exfil FQDN.

Transitive install of poisoned @injectivelabs 1.20.21 build under node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Structural supply-chain detection: the campaign-unique build filenames accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js appearing under a node_modules/@injectivelabs path. Resilient to re-signing/re-hash because it keys on the version-marker filenames + package scope rather than the SHA-256, catching victims who pulled the stealer transitively via any of the 18 sibling packages. Rationale: The build filenames accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js are unique to the poisoned 1.20.21 dist and act as a version marker; combined with the node_modules/@injectivelabs scope this flags transitive victims (e.g. via wallet-core) who never named sdk-ts directly, and survives re-hash of the still-downloadable deprecated package.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Aikido/other scanner replaying the artifact during a rescan
  • Developer intentionally checking out the compromised version to reproduce/analyze
  • A future clean @injectivelabs build coincidentally reusing the same hashed chunk name (unlikely — Rollup chunk hashes are content-derived)
Response runbook
1) Triage: on each hit, read the package's package.json version and lockfile to confirm 1.20.21 was resolved (directly or transitively). 2) Contain: delete node_modules, repin @injectivelabs/* to >=1.20.23, and rebuild; flag any wallet keys/seed phrases derived on the host for rotation. 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo/CI job with @injectivelabs/*@1.20.21 in lockfiles and correlate hosts against exfil-domain contacts and the SHA-256 file detection.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs", "accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
| where FolderPath contains "node_modules" and FolderPath contains "injectivelabs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs", "accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
| where TargetFilePath contains "node_modules" and TargetFilePath contains "injectivelabs"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-09 16 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

GigaWiper, also tracked as BLUERABBIT, is a destructive backdoor that combines multiple wiping and ransomware-like capabilities into a single operational platform. This blog analyzes how the malware incorporates code from several previously separate malware families and provides guidance to help defenders detect and defend against similar threats. The post GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GigaWiper persistence: 'OneDrive Update' scheduled task run-every-minute · [LLM] GigaWiper persistence marker: HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment counter · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GigaWiper C2: RabbitMQ/Redis connection to 185.182.193.21:5544/7542 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GigaWiper destructive Golang backdoor/wiper by known SHA-256 · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
GigaWiper destructive Golang backdoor/wiper by known SHA-256 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts execution, drop, or load of the five Microsoft-published GigaWiper backdoor and standalone-wiper binaries. High-fidelity because these hashes are the destructive tooling itself (raw-disk wipe, Crucio-derived fake ransomware, FlockWiper re-implementation) - a single hit is an active destruction event. Rationale: Uses the five exact SHA-256 IOCs Microsoft published (Table 2) for the GigaWiper backdoor and standalone wiper; a hash match is unambiguous destructive tooling. Architecture corroborated by Binary Defense's BLUERABBIT (same RabbitMQ+Redis+dual-wiper design). Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/the-anatomy-of-wiper-malware-part-1/
ATT&CKT1485 T1561.002 T1561.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or IR team detonating a sample in a lab that reports to the same tenant
  • Threat-intel/EDR test harness deliberately dropping the IOC hashes to validate detections
  • Security vendor scan uploading the sample to a scanning appliance on the network
  • Re-hash collision is not credible for SHA-256, so genuine benign hits are near-zero
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malwarelab","detonation") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cuckoo.exe","procdump.exe"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the hash match and check DeviceProcessEvents for the process tree and whether WipeMain / schtasks 'OneDrive Update' / connections to 185.182.193.21 already followed - if any did, treat as live destruction, not a scan. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately network-isolate the host via Defender, force-block the five hashes tenant-wide, and snapshot/preserve any still-intact disks before the wiper reboots them. 3) HUNT: Sweep the tenant for the other four hashes, the 'OneDrive Update' task, HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment, and outbound traffic to 185.182.193.21:5544/7542 to find other beachheads before the fanout 'All' exchange broadcasts a wipe command.

GigaWiper persistence: 'OneDrive Update' scheduled task run-every-minute AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of GigaWiper's persistence task, a schtasks invocation that registers a task literally named 'OneDrive Update' scheduled to run every minute plus at startup. Article-specific: real OneDrive uses tasks named 'OneDrive Standalone Update Task' under OneDrive.exe, never a per-minute 'OneDrive Update'. Rationale: Pins on the exact task name 'OneDrive Update' plus the per-minute schedule from the article's Figure 3 persistence command, and excludes genuine OneDrive updater parents - the masquerade name is the high-fidelity anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal software-distribution or RMM tool that names a custom task 'OneDrive Update' (rare; usually branded to the vendor)
  • Admin manually recreating a broken OneDrive updater task with a non-standard name
  • GPO/Intune deployment scripting a OneDrive keep-alive task per minute (should originate from a known deployment parent - allowlist it)
  • Backup/monitoring agent creating a minute-cadence task with 'OneDrive' in the name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Microsoft OneDrive\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "AppData\\Local\\Microsoft\\OneDrive"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the task XML (schtasks /query /tn 'OneDrive Update' /xml) and the InitiatingProcess hash - if the action points to an unsigned Golang PE or a non-OneDrive path, escalate. 2) CONTAIN: Delete the task (schtasks /delete /tn 'OneDrive Update' /f), isolate the host, and block the initiating binary's hash. 3) HUNT: Check HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment execution-counter value on this and peer hosts, and query for the five GigaWiper hashes and 185.182.193.21 connections to scope the intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("/create", "OneDrive Update")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/sc minute", "/sc onstart", "minute")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe", "OneDriveSetup.exe", "OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe", "msiexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has_all ("/create", "OneDrive Update")
| where CommandLine has_any ("/sc minute", "/sc onstart", "minute")
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "\\OneDrive.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GigaWiper C2: RabbitMQ/Redis connection to 185.182.193.21:5544/7542 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to GigaWiper's hard-coded C2 host 185.182.193.21 on the RabbitMQ (AMQP 5544) and Redis (7542) ports it uses for command receipt and result upload. Article-specific: workstation processes speaking AMQP/Redis to a public IP on these non-standard ports is the backdoor's C2 heartbeat. Rationale: Uses Microsoft's exact hard-coded C2 IP 185.182.193.21 (ports 5544 RabbitMQ / 7542 Redis). The RabbitMQ-tasking + Redis-state design is independently corroborated by Binary Defense's BLUERABBIT, raising confidence in the pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities
ATT&CKT1071 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst or sinkhole researcher intentionally probing 185.182.193.21 from a monitored host
  • Firewall/IDS appliance sourcing a block-verification connection to the IOC IP
  • Shared-hosting reuse: the IP is later reassigned to a benign service (validate WHOIS/passive-DNS before trusting a stale IOC)
  • Legitimate internal RabbitMQ/Redis on a different IP is unaffected - this pins the specific malicious IP, not the ports alone
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify InitiatingProcess/ContextImageFileName making the connection - an unsigned Golang PE or a process also matching the GigaWiper hashes confirms C2. 2) CONTAIN: Block 185.182.193.21 at the firewall/EDR, isolate the beaconing host, and preserve memory before reboot (the wiper forces an immediate restart). 3) HUNT: Because commands publish to the fanout 'All' exchange (broadcast to every infected client), assume multiple hosts - sweep the tenant for any traffic to 185.182.193.21, the 'OneDrive Update' task, and the five GigaWiper hashes to enumerate all bots before a wipe is issued.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "185.182.193.21"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "185.182.193.21"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetworkProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GigaWiper persistence marker: HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment counter AIInstallation Medium
Hunts writes to GigaWiper's execution-count registry value under HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment by a process that is not the genuine OneDrive client. Article-specific: real OneDrive stores state under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive, so a bare SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment key is a masqueraded first-run/run-count marker. Rationale: Anchors on the exact masqueraded persistence key HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment from the article, excluding genuine OneDrive writers - distinct from the real HKCU\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive path, so hits are high-fidelity. Falcon left empty: this non-ASEP HKCU value is not carried by FDR's AsepValueUpdate autostart telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities
ATT&CKT1112 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party OneDrive management/backup utility that writes state under a non-Microsoft OneDrive key
  • Legacy or renamed OneDrive build writing to SOFTWARE\OneDrive rather than SOFTWARE\Microsoft\OneDrive
  • Admin/registry-cleanup tooling touching an orphaned OneDrive key during troubleshooting
  • Endpoint-management agent snapshotting HKCU hives and re-writing values (writer would be the agent, not a Golang PE)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Microsoft OneDrive\\"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the value data (it should be a small integer run-counter) and the writing process hash - correlate against the GigaWiper hash list and the 'OneDrive Update' task on the same host. 2) CONTAIN: If the writer is unsigned/Golang or hash-matched, isolate the host, delete the key, remove the task, and block the binary. 3) HUNT: The key is set to '0' on first run and incremented each scheduled execution - hosts with value > 0 have run repeatedly; pivot on those plus 185.182.193.21 traffic to find long-dwell infections.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe", "OneDriveSetup.exe", "OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment"
| where ActingProcessName !has "OneDrive.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Scheduled Task Creation with Suspicious Image / Encoded Args
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0d
status: experimental
description: |
    schtasks.exe /create with payload-shaped action — points at
    powershell, cmd, rundll32, encoded-base64, or user-writable paths.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1053.005
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_schtasks:
        Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: '/create'
    selection_payload:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'powershell'
            - 'cmd.exe'
            - 'rundll32'
            - '-enc'
            - 'FromBase64'
            - '\Users\Public'
            - '\AppData\'
    condition: selection_schtasks and selection_payload
falsepositives:
    - GPO-driven scheduled tasks, MDT/SCCM imaging
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd") or SHA1 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd") or MD5 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd") or SHA1 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd") or MD5 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_hash

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.process_hash IN ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_hash

Article-specific behavioural hunt — GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware Exploitation High
Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("mc.exe", "wevutil.exe", "node.js") or FolderPath has_any ("C:\ProgramData\output", "C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\Security.evtx", "A:\GRAT\CWipeNew\Release\CWipeNew.pdb", "E:\files\new\GRAT\CWipe\Release\CWipe.pdb"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("C:\ProgramData\output", "C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\Security.evtx", "A:\GRAT\CWipeNew\Release\CWipeNew.pdb", "E:\files\new\GRAT\CWipe\Release\CWipe.pdb") or FileName in~ ("mc.exe", "wevutil.exe", "node.js"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,

China and India ran separate espionage operations against the same Pakistani police force, each drawn by different stakes in Pakistan's internal security.
