Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — One Target, Two Flags | Rival Espionage Actors Converge On Pakistani Law Enforce
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/Remcos infrastructure targeting Pakistani law enforcement · [LLM] Compromised web-application server beaconing to espionage C2 (portal-update implant) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Outbound C2 to PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/Remcos infrastructure targeting Pakistani law enforcement AICommand & Control High
Hunts any internal host establishing outbound connections to the 13 C2 IPs SentinelLABS attributed to the four tooling clusters (PlugX, ShadowPad, Cobalt Strike, Remcos) converging on Balochistan Police and other Pakistani law-enforcement orgs between Feb 2024 and Apr 2026. Pure network-IOC match on disclosed espionage C2 servers. Rationale: Anchored on the exact 13 C2 IPs from Table 1 / code blocks (PlugX 172.111.233.x + 172.94.9.x + 45.74.6.17, ShadowPad 45.125.32.218, Cobalt Strike 142.171.183.8 + 193.42.25.65, Remcos 89.31.121.220). Any egress to these known-bad hosts is high-fidelity; the tooling families and Pakistani-entity victimology are corroborated externally, though the specific IPs are from the SentinelLABS primary report only. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.shadowpad • https://thehackernews.com/2023/07/pakistani-entities-targeted-in.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / threat-intel analyst deliberately sandboxing or sinkholing one of these IPs from a corporate host
  • IP reassignment after takedown — a benign service later hosted on a recycled VPS IP (172.94.9.x / 45.x hosting ranges are commodity VPS)
  • Internal threat-intel validation tooling or EDR connectivity checks pinging the IOC list
  • Proxy/NAT concentration causing many internal hosts to appear as one src toward the IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") // exclude EDR/AV connectivity-check processes
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the connection is genuinely outbound and established (not a blocked/attempt), identify the initiating process and host role — servers hosting the CMS/FIR/HRMIS/HotelEye/CRMS apps are highest priority. 2) Contain: block all 13 IPs at perimeter, isolate the host, snapshot memory before reboot to preserve PlugX/ShadowPad in-memory implants. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for DLL side-loading (unsigned DLL next to a signed EXE), scheduled tasks/Run keys created near first-seen, and lateral SMB/RDP from the host; sweep the org for any other host touching the same /24s (172.111.233.0/24, 172.94.9.0/24).

| where RemoteIP in (C2)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc

Compromised web-application server beaconing to espionage C2 (portal-update implant) AICommand & Control Medium
Tighter server-side pivot: a web/application-server process (IIS w3wp, Apache/Tomcat java, nginx, php-cgi) on a Pakistani law-enforcement web server initiating outbound to the disclosed C2 IPs. Grounds on the article's China-nexus 'custom implants masquerading as a portal update' planted in one of the citizen/police web applications (e.g. the Complaint Management System). Rationale: Combines the exact C2 IP set with a server-process filter to isolate the article's specific scenario — a China-nexus implant planted in a citizen/police web application (CMS) beaconing out. Web-server processes reaching commodity-VPS C2 IPs is extremely rare and high-fidelity, and directly targets the compromised-webapp vector the article calls out. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.shadowpad
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1505.003 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web app legitimately calling an outbound API that happens to be on a recycled VPS IP after IOC takedown
  • Java-based agent/monitoring on the web server making outbound telemetry calls
  • Server-side update/package fetch (Tomcat/Maven, php composer) to a mirror on the same hosting range
  • App-server health-check or CDN origin-pull to a reassigned address
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "maven" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "composer" // exclude server package-manager fetches
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which web application the process serves (CMS/FIR/HRMIS/AVLS/HotelEye/CRMS) and whether the beacon started after a recent 'portal update'/deployment window; review web-root for recently modified/added handler, JSP, ASPX or PHP files. 2) Contain: take the web app offline or block egress, preserve IIS/Tomcat logs and web-root for forensics, rotate app/service and DB credentials the server can reach. 3) Hunt: search web access logs (W3CIISLog/AppServiceHTTPLogs) for the implant's request pattern, look for webshell-style POSTs, and pivot to any DB export or biometric/criminal-record access from the compromised app identity.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time

| sort - count

Symlinks Are Still Scary (And Yes, You Can Commit Them to Git)

Snyk
2026-07-09 5 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A harmless-looking symlink in a Git repo can redirect a tool into reading or writing anywhere on your machine. That old trick is now showing up in AI coding assistants, with nasty results.

CVEsCVE-2026-12958 CVE-2026-50549 CVE-2024-32002 CVE-2024-21626 CVE-2021-32803
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Git-spawned hook execution during recursive clone (CVE-2024-32002) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SSH authorized_keys written by non-SSH tooling (symlink repo payload) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Symlinks Are Still Scary (And Yes, You Can Commit Them to Git)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SSH authorized_keys written by non-SSH tooling (symlink repo payload) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts writes/modifications to any user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys where the writing process is NOT legitimate SSH provisioning tooling — the payoff of the article's headline attack, where a symlink named like project_settings.json checked out from a cloned repo resolves to authorized_keys and a build script/editor/AI coding agent silently writes an attacker key through it. Because the OS resolves the symlink transparently, the file event reports the real target path (.ssh/authorized_keys), which is the tell. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact payload path ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (code Block 1) written by non-SSH tooling — the symlink resolves so the OS reports the real target, making the write-through observable. Cross-checked MITRE T1098.004, Splunk Security Content and Elastic authorized_keys rules to confirm the technique and avoid duplicating a generic FIM rule by scoping on the writing process. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/004/ • https://research.splunk.com/endpoint/f5ab595e-28e5-4327-8077-5008ba97c850/ • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/cross-platform/persistence_ssh_authorized_keys_modification
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible/Puppet/Salt/Terraform pushing authorized_keys via a config-management run (excluded, but custom wrappers may slip through)
  • Developer legitimately running ssh-copy-id or manually editing authorized_keys with vim/nano
  • Cloud-init / provisioning agent seeding keys on first boot of a new VM
  • CI runner injecting a deploy key into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as an intended step
  • Dotfile-management tools (chezmoi, GNU stow) that symlink or template SSH config
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("terraform","authorized_keys_command","chezmoi","stow") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ansible"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess chain — is the writer a dev tool (git, node, python, code, cursor) or shell spawned from a freshly cloned repo path? Compare the written key fingerprint against the user's known keys and check if the file is/was a symlink (ls -l ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, readlink). 2) Contain: if the key is unrecognized, remove the offending authorized_keys line, kill active sessions authenticated by it, and rotate the account; quarantine the source repo. 3) Hunt: search the same host/user for the source symlink (git ls-files -s | grep '^120000'), other writes to ~/.ssh, ~/.bashrc, ~/.git/hooks, and any inbound SSH logons using the added key.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath endswith "/.ssh/authorized_keys" or (FileName == "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sshd","ssh","ssh-keygen","ssh-copy-id","cloud-init","useradd","adduser","ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFilePath endswith "/.ssh/authorized_keys" or (TargetFileName == "authorized_keys" and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRename")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("sshd","ssh-keygen","ssh-copy-id","cloud-init","ansible","puppet","salt-minion"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SSH authorized_keys Written by Non-SSH Tooling (Symlink Repo Payload)
id: 5c2e6b1a-9f3d-4a77-8b0e-2d1c6f9a4e21
description: Detects creation or modification of a user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys by a process that is not legitimate SSH provisioning tooling, consistent with a symlink committed to a cloned git repository resolving to authorized_keys and being written through by a build script, editor, or AI coding agent.
references:
  - https://snyk.io/blog/symlinks-are-still-scary/
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/004/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1098.004
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '/.ssh/authorized_keys'
  filter_legit:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sshd'
      - '/ssh-keygen'
      - '/ssh-copy-id'
      - '/cloud-init'
      - '/ansible'
      - '/salt-minion'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*authorized_keys* AND (*">>"* OR *tee* OR *">"*)) -@process.executable.path:(*/sshd OR */ssh-keygen OR */ssh-copy-id OR */cloud-init)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\/\.ssh\/authorized_keys$/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\/(sshd|ssh-keygen|ssh-copy-id|cloud-init)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/authorized_keys" Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified","renamed") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action Filesystem.process_guid
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Git-spawned hook execution during recursive clone (CVE-2024-32002) AIExploitation High
Hunts a process whose image lives inside a .git/hooks/ directory and whose parent is git — the exact signature of CVE-2024-32002, where a malicious repository's crafted submodule + symlink writes a hook into .git/ that git executes while the clone is still running, yielding RCE from nothing more than git clone --recurse-submodules. No build step or 'run the project' required. Rationale: Anchored on the CVE-2024-32002 mechanic named in the article (git clone --recurse-submodules dropping a script into .git/hooks and running it during clone). The parent=git + child-image-in-.git/hooks pair is high-fidelity because hooks are not supposed to execute during a clone; confirmed via the git security advisory GHSA-8h77-4q3w-gfgv and Amal Murali's PoC writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/git/git/security/advisories/GHSA-8h77-4q3w-gfgv • https://amalmurali.me/posts/git-rce/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2024/05/16/git-cve-2024-32002/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer with legitimately installed local git hooks (post-checkout/post-merge) firing during a normal pull or checkout
  • Husky / pre-commit framework hooks that shell out during commit or checkout operations
  • CI systems that intentionally invoke repo hooks as part of a pipeline stage
  • git-lfs post-checkout smudge hooks running on a large-file repo clone
  • Monorepo tooling (e.g. Nx, Turborepo) that registers checkout hooks
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("husky","git-lfs","post-merge") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pull","checkout HEAD","lfs"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the executed hook file under .git/hooks/ and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm it was a clone/--recurse-submodules op and read the hook body for network callbacks or key writes. Check git version on host against the patched set (>=2.39.4/2.40.2/2.41.1/2.42.2/2.43.4/2.44.1/2.45.1). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the hook process tree, and quarantine the cloned repo directory; block the source repo URL. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for downstream child processes of the hook, writes to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, new persistence (cron, systemd units, shell rc files), and outbound C2 from the hook's PID.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.git/hooks/", "\\.git\\hooks\\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","git.exe","git-remote-https","git-remote-https.exe","bash","sh","dash")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","submodule","--recurse-submodules") or FolderPath has_any ("post-checkout","post-clone","post-update")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/.git/hooks/", "\\.git\\hooks\\")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("git","bash","sh","dash")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","submodule","--recurse-submodules") or ActingProcessName has_any ("post-checkout","post-clone","post-update")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joro proxy-mode confused-deputy: browser POSTs to loopback API 127.0.0.1:9090 (CVE-2026-53649) AIDelivery Low
Hunts a web browser process opening connections to the Joro proxy-mode API on loopback TCP/9090, the confused-deputy vector CVE-2026-53649 abuses when attacker-controlled cross-origin JavaScript reaches the unauthenticated, wildcard-CORS Joro API. Article-specific because it pins the exact bind (127.0.0.1:9090) and the browser-mediated initiator. Rationale: Uses the exact loopback bind (127.0.0.1:9090) named in the advisory plus a browser-process initiator, the confused-deputy shape of CVE-2026-53649. Deliberately hunting/Low because a legitimate Joro operator's own browser talks to the same UI/API port. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling • https://github.com/bishopfox
ATT&CKT1189 T1204.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Joro operator using the proxy-mode web UI, which itself talks to 127.0.0.1:9090
  • Unrelated local dev services on 9090 (Prometheus Pushgateway, SonarQube, custom app) that a browser hits
  • Browser DevTools/extension polling a localhost dev server on the same port
  • Local reverse-proxy or API mock bound to 9090 during development
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Joro is installed/running on the host and whether the operator was actively using the Joro UI at that timestamp; pull the browser history for the immediately preceding external navigation. 2) Contain: if the loopback hit was NOT operator-initiated UI use, kill the joro process, isolate the host, and block the external page's domain at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot to whether joro subsequently wrote a .so plugin, restarted, or spawned an interactive shell (see companion UCs) — that sequence confirms exploitation.

| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("firefox","firefox-bin","chrome","chromium","msedge","brave","Google Chrome","Firefox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc

Joro native plugin RCE: joro process spawns interactive /bin/bash shell (CVE-2026-53649) AIExploitation High
Alerts when the joro binary spawns an interactive Unix shell (bash/sh/dash/zsh with -i), the terminal step of the CVE-2026-53649 chain where a malicious uploaded plugin's init() opens a goroutine and yields an interactive /bin/bash -i shell as the operator's user. High fidelity because joro is a proxy/teamserver, not a shell launcher — it has no legitimate reason to fork a local login shell. Rationale: Pins the article's exact parent (joro) and payload (interactive /bin/bash -i obtained on plugin.Open() init()). Because Joro is a proxy that never legitimately forks a local login shell, parent=joro + shell + -i is a near-zero-FP RCE tell. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.004 T1129
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Joro developer/operator debugging the tool and manually shelling out from a plugin during testing
  • A local wrapper or helper script also named 'joro' that legitimately invokes a shell
  • Operator running a benign self-authored plugin that spawns a shell for tooling
  • CI/build harness building Joro plugins that exec a shell as part of a test
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child shell's full process tree and any sockets it holds (ss -p); confirm the joro process previously loaded a newly-written .so and restarted. 2) Contain: kill the shell and joro process, isolate the host, and snapshot /proc for the joro PID before termination for the loaded-plugin path. 3) Hunt: enumerate the Joro plugin directory for attacker-uploaded .so files, review recent POSTs to /api/v1/plugins/upload and /api/v1/system/restart, and check outbound connections from joro to external hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "joro"
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-i"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where TargetProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ash")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "-i"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joro writes a native .so plugin: attacker plugin drop before restart (CVE-2026-53649) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the joro process writing a shared-object (.so) plugin file to disk, the staging step where CVE-2026-53649's unauthenticated upload endpoint persists an attacker-supplied native plugin that executes its init() on the next plugin.Open(). Article-specific via the joro-process writer plus the .so plugin artifact. Rationale: Ties the article's plugin-upload artifact (a native .so consumed by plugin.Open()) to the joro process as writer. joro dropping a .so it did not build interactively is the on-disk footprint of the upload endpoint being abused. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling
ATT&CKT1129 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator legitimately installing/updating a Joro plugin through the intended workflow
  • Joro's own --build-plugin feature emitting a compiled .so during plugin development
  • Package manager or updater refreshing bundled Joro plugins on the same host
  • Backup/sync tooling restoring the Joro plugin directory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the written .so, submit to sandbox/AV, and check whether it was preceded by a browser hit to 127.0.0.1:9090 and a joro restart. 2) Contain: quarantine the .so, stop joro before it re-opens the plugin, and isolate the host if the file is unsigned/unknown. 3) Hunt: look for joro spawning an interactive shell or making outbound public connections after the write, and sweep other operator hosts for the same .so hash (one ABI-matched plugin works against every operator on the release).

| where FileName endswith ".so"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Nuclio CronJob container args carry injected shell (CVE-2026-52831 header/body OS command injection)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Orphaned Nuclio CronJob without ownerReferences (CVE-2026-52831 persistence) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-52831: Nuclio: Unsanitized cron trigger event headers
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Nuclio cron pod shell reads Kubernetes service-account token (CVE-2026-52831 credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Nuclio CronJob container args carry injected shell (CVE-2026-52831 header/body OS command injection) AIExploitation High
Hunts Kubernetes API audit events that create/update a CronJob whose container args are the Nuclio '/bin/sh -c curl ...' string but also contain shell metacharacters or a service-account-token read — the signature of CVE-2026-52831 header-key/body command injection. Nuclio's legitimate cron CronJob is a pure curl invocation, so any command substitution or ';' break inside those args is exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact injection sink: CronJob container args = '/bin/sh -c curl --silent --header ...' (lazy.go:2212). A benign Nuclio cron job is a pure curl, so command-substitution ('$('), a ';'-broken header, '&&', backticks, or a serviceaccount/token read inside those args is unambiguous CVE-2026-52831 exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5px-423j-pf7p • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/nuclio/nuclio/CVE-2026-52831/ • https://corgea.com/advisories/packages/go/github.com/nuclio/nuclio
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Nuclio operator legitimately sets a curl '--data' body that happens to contain a literal '$(' as text (rare, but possible in templated payloads)
  • An admin manually editing a CronJob to add a debug '&& echo' step during troubleshooting
  • Third-party K8s tooling that wraps curl health-checks in '/bin/sh -c' with chained commands in the same namespace
  • A custom (non-Nuclio) CronJob that legitimately reads the service-account token and pipes it to curl for an in-cluster API call
Suppression filter
| where not (ReqStr has "nuclio.io/skip-scan")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the flagged CronJob's full args from the audit RequestObject; identify the injected command after the header break or inside '$()'. Trace back to the NuclioFunction trigger spec (event.headers key / event.body) that seeded it and the user/service-account that applied it. 2) Contain: 'kubectl delete cronjob <name> -n <namespace>' immediately (it has NO ownerReferences so it will NOT cascade-delete), suspend the parent NuclioFunction, and rotate the pod's service-account token if the injected command read it. 3) Hunt: enumerate all CronJobs in the nuclio namespace for the same markers, review kube-apiserver audit for other create/patch calls from the same actor, and check egress from cron pods to unexpected hosts.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "cronjobs"
| where Stage == "ResponseComplete"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has "/bin/sh" and ReqStr has "curl"
| where ReqStr has_any ("$(", "; id", "; echo", "serviceaccount/token", "&&", "| sh", "`")
| extend Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), CronJobName = tostring(ObjectRef.name), Actor = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Verb, Namespace, CronJobName, Actor, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.resource:cronjobs @requestObject.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.containers.args:*serviceaccount/token*
CLOUD
index=* (sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" OR sourcetype="kube_audit") verb IN (create,update,patch) objectRef.resource=cronjobs
| spath output=cargs path=requestObject.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.containers{}.args{}
| eval cargs=mvjoin(cargs," ")
| where match(cargs,"/bin/sh") AND match(cargs,"curl")
| where match(cargs,"\$\(") OR match(cargs,";\s*id") OR match(cargs,";\s*echo") OR match(cargs,"serviceaccount/token") OR match(cargs,"&&") OR match(cargs,"\|\s*sh") OR match(cargs,"`")
| table _time objectRef.namespace objectRef.name user.username cargs
| sort - _time
Nuclio cron pod shell reads Kubernetes service-account token (CVE-2026-52831 credential theft) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the runtime side of CVE-2026-52831: a shell process assembled from a Nuclio cron curl command ('curl --silent --header ...') that also reads /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token or contains '$()' command substitution. This is the injected payload actually executing and stealing the pod's cluster credential. Rationale: Anchors on the PoC payload strings — '/bin/sh -c curl --silent --header ...' plus the injected 'cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token' recon (article Step 6). The curl+header signature scopes to Nuclio cron pods; the token read or '$()' is the injected command running, making this high-fidelity credential-access telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5px-423j-pf7p • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/nuclio/nuclio/CVE-2026-52831/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Nuclio function whose curl body deliberately embeds shell-like text that survives into the command line
  • In-cluster health-check scripts that both curl an endpoint and echo the SA token for debugging
  • Security scanners / CIS benchmark tools that intentionally read the service-account token path to test exposure
  • A developer manually exec-ing into a cron pod and running a chained curl + id for troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "nuclio.io/debug"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and the host/pod; confirm the parent is a Nuclio cron container and decode any '$()' substitution to see what executed. Determine whether the SA token was actually exfiltrated (look for the token value flowing into a subsequent curl to an external host). 2) Contain: cordon/evict the pod, delete the offending CronJob and parent NuclioFunction, and immediately rotate the compromised service-account token (delete the secret / bounce the SA). 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents/NetworkConnectIP4 from the pod for outbound C2, search for the stolen token being used against the kube-apiserver, and sweep other nuclio pods for the same shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has "--header"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token", "$(", "; id", "; echo")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--header"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token", "$(", "; id", "; echo")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Orphaned Nuclio CronJob without ownerReferences (CVE-2026-52831 persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts Nuclio-generated CronJobs (name prefix 'nuclio-cron-job-') created/updated without any ownerReferences. Per the advisory, these carry no owner link to the NuclioFunction so Kubernetes cascade deletion never removes them — a controller crash leaves the injected CronJob executing on schedule indefinitely, the article's stated persistence mechanism. Rationale: Uses the article's exact artifact naming ('nuclio-cron-job-<id>', Step 7 output) and the documented root cause at lazy.go:522 — Nuclio CronJobs carry no ownerReferences. An orphaned nuclio-cron-job-* is precisely the persistence primitive the advisory warns survives function deletion. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5px-423j-pf7p • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/nuclio/nuclio/CVE-2026-52831/
ATT&CKT1053.007
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal Nuclio behaviour — by design these CronJobs lack ownerReferences, so every legit cron trigger fires this (baseline the expected set)
  • A CronJob captured mid-update where the audit snapshot predates owner attachment
  • Manually GitOps-managed nuclio CronJobs whose ownerReferences are stripped by a sync tool
  • Restored-from-backup CronJobs that lost their owner linkage
Response runbook
1) Triage: since ALL Nuclio cron CronJobs legitimately lack ownerReferences, cross-reference each 'nuclio-cron-job-*' against currently-existing NuclioFunctions — flag any CronJob with no live parent function as a true orphan. Inspect its container args for the CVE-2026-52831 injection markers. 2) Contain: delete confirmed orphan CronJobs ('kubectl delete cronjob'), as cascade will not remove them; upgrade Nuclio to the fixed build (0.0.0-20260601075854-3356b86a8bfa or later). 3) Hunt: diff the CronJob inventory against the NuclioFunction inventory on a schedule to catch future orphans, and correlate orphan creation timestamps with any controller crash/restart events.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Verb in ("create","update")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "cronjobs"
| extend CronJobName = tostring(ObjectRef.name)
| where CronJobName startswith "nuclio-cron-job-"
| extend Owners = RequestObject.metadata.ownerReferences
| where isnull(Owners) or array_length(todynamic(Owners)) == 0
| extend Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), Actor = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Verb, Namespace, CronJobName, Actor
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update) @objectRef.resource:cronjobs @objectRef.name:nuclio-cron-job-* -@requestObject.metadata.ownerReferences.uid:*
CLOUD
index=* (sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" OR sourcetype="kube_audit") verb IN (create,update) objectRef.resource=cronjobs objectRef.name=nuclio-cron-job-*
| spath output=owners path=requestObject.metadata.ownerReferences{}.uid
| where isnull(owners)
| table _time objectRef.namespace objectRef.name user.username
| sort - _time

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] PromptSpy dropper APK sample hash landing on monitored endpoint · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] PromptSpy Android GenAI malware C2/distribution domain contact (mgardownload.com, m-mgarg.com) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
PromptSpy Android GenAI malware C2/distribution domain contact (mgardownload.com, m-mgarg.com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts network/DNS resolution of the two PromptSpy domains named in ESET's H1 2026 report: mgardownload[.]com (served the malicious 'MorganArg'/JPMorgan-themed dropper APK) and m-mgarg[.]com (webpage opened post-install, staging the VNC/Gemini C2 flow). Any corporate DNS resolver, proxy, or MDM-managed device touching these is a PromptSpy indicator, not a generic beacon template. Rationale: Both domains are explicitly attributed to PromptSpy by ESET's dedicated write-up (VirusTotal shows all four droppers served from mgardownload[.]com; the dropper opens m-mgarg[.]com on launch) and confirmed by The Hacker News / Cybersecurity News, so they are high-fidelity and non-generic. Dropped the AWS/Cloudflare IPs (54.67.2.84, 52.222.205.45, 104.21.91.170) as shared hosting with no second-source PromptSpy attribution. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/promptspy-ushers-in-era-android-threats-using-genai/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/02/promptspy-android-malware-abuses-google.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/promptspy-android-ai-malware/ • https://github.com/eset/malware-ioc
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or TI enrichment tooling (URLScan, VirusTotal, ANY.RUN) resolving the domain from a lab/analyst workstation during IOC research
  • Passive-DNS / sinkhole collectors that log resolutions of known-bad domains
  • Security web proxy that pre-resolves URLs in blocked email for detonation
  • Managed Android (MDM/Intune) test device intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox VLAN
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the querying host/user and whether it is an analyst/sandbox asset or a real user endpoint; check if the resolution succeeded and whether any follow-on connection to the returned IP occurred. For Android, pull MDM inventory for a 'MorganArg'/JPMorgan-lookalike package. 2) Contain: sink-hole/block both domains at DNS and proxy; if a managed device, isolate it and initiate mobile-threat-defense scan; block the resolved IPs at egress. 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolved IPs across DeviceNetworkEvents/firewall for other internal talkers, search DeviceFileEvents/download logs for the APK sample SHA1s (see companion UC), and review any VNC-style outbound sessions from mobile subnets.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("mgardownload.com","m-mgarg.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
 (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where Name has_any ("mgardownload.com","m-mgarg.com")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIP=ClientIP, Domain=Name),
 (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationDnsDomain has_any ("mgardownload.com","m-mgarg.com") or RequestURL has_any ("mgardownload.com","m-mgarg.com")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, Domain=coalesce(DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PromptSpy dropper APK sample hash landing on monitored endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the nine PromptSpy dropper APK SHA1 hashes from the ESET H1 2026 IOC bundle appearing in file telemetry — e.g. an APK downloaded to a Windows workstation/file share for sideloading, staged on a jump box, or synced from mobile backup. Exact-hash match, so any hit is the actual sample, not a lookalike. Rationale: The nine SHA1 values are the ESET-published PromptSpy dropper samples (mirrored in the eset/malware-ioc GitHub repo and VirusTotal), so an exact match is unambiguous. Detection is on file telemetry because these are Android APKs that won't execute as Windows processes — they only surface if the sample is downloaded/staged on a monitored endpoint or file share. Datadog/Falcon left empty: neither reliably carries file-write SHA1 for non-executed APKs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/eset/malware-ioc • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/promptspy-ushers-in-era-android-threats-using-genai/
ATT&CKT1105 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst deliberately downloading/storing the PromptSpy sample on a lab or research workstation
  • EDR/AV quarantine or backup copy of the sample retaining the original hash
  • Threat-intel sample-repo sync (MISP, internal malware zoo) landing files on a collector host
  • IR responder copying a captured sample to a case-evidence share
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "\\Quarantine\\" or FolderPath has "\\MalwareSamples\\" or FolderPath has "\\Evidence\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host role — analyst/lab/evidence host vs. a normal user endpoint; inspect FolderPath and FileOriginUrl to see whether it arrived via download (mgardownload[.]com) vs. a research tool, and identify the acquiring user/process. 2) Contain: if a production user endpoint, isolate it, delete/quarantine the APK, and check for onward transfer to any Android device via USB/MDM sideload; block the source URL. 3) Hunt: pivot the FileOriginUrl and downloading host into the companion domain-resolution UC, sweep other endpoints/file shares for the same SHA1 set, and review mobile fleet for the installed 'MorganArg'/JPMorgan-lookalike package.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac") or SHA1 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac") or MD5 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac") or SHA1 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac") or MD5 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vidar Stealer Unmasked: Code Signing Abuse, Go Loaders and File Inflation

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-07-07 14 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A cybercrime campaign combined a loader-as-a-service framework and DLL sideloading via a Go-compiled fake MpClient.dll, a novel evasion layer combination. The post Vidar Stealer Unmasked: Code Signing Abuse, Go Loaders and File Inflation appeared first on Unit 42 .
